question.explanation:
The stationary points of a multivariable function $f$ are the points $\mathbf a$ in the domain of $f$ such that $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) =\mathbf 0^T,$ where \[ \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \left.\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \end{bmatrix}\right|_{\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a}}. \]

In tihs case, the domain of $f$ is $\mathbb{R}^2,$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are \begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= 4x + 4y\\[5pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= 4x + 2y + 4. \end{align*}

So, the first derivative of $f$ is \[ \boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \begin{bmatrix} 4x + 4y & 4x + 2y + 4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

To find the stationary points, we need to find the points where $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf{0}^T.$ Setting $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf{0}^T,$ we have the following system: \[ \begin{cases} 4x + 4y = 0 \\[5pt] 4x + 2y + 4 = 0 \end{cases} \]

Solving for $x$ in the first equation, we get \[ 4x+4y=0 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad x = -y. \]

Then, substituting $x = -y$ into the second equation, we get \[ \begin{align*} 4(-y) + 2y +4&= 0 \\[5pt] -4y + 2y + 4 &= 0 \\[5pt] -2y &= -4\\[5pt] y &= 2. \end{align*} \]

Back-substituting this value into $x=-y,$ we obtain \[ y=2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = -2. \]

Therefore, our system has one solution, $(-2,2).$

In conclusion, $f$ has one stationary point, $(-2,2).$

example.title: Finding the Critical Points of a Function

question.text:
The function $ f(x,y) % = \sin{x} \sin{y} $ has the second derivative \[ \boldsymbol f''(x,y) = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin{x} \sin{y} & \cos{x} \cos{y} \\ \cos{x} \cos{y} & -\sin{x} \sin{y} \end{bmatrix} \] and has a stationary point at $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

  1. $H\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) < 0$
  2. $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) > 0$
  3. The point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ is a local maximum of $f$
question.explanation:
The second partial derivative test states that if $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(\mathbf a),$ we have the following:

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) > 0,$ then:

    • if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $\mathbf{a}$

    • if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) >0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $\mathbf{a}$

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $\mathbf{a}$

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) = 0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

Evaluating the second derivative at $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),$ we obtain

\begin{align*} \boldsymbol f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Now, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of $\boldsymbol f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),$ we get \[ H\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \det\left(\boldsymbol f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) = (-1)^2 - 0^2 = 1 > 0. \]

  • Statement II is false. We have $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \left(\boldsymbol f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right)_{11} = -1 \lt 0.$

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) > 0$ and $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) < 0,$ the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

example.title: Classifying a Critical Point Using the Second Partial Derivatives Test

question.text: Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function $ f(x,y) % = x^3 -6xy + y^3 $ given that \[ \boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \begin{bmatrix} \ln y& \dfrac x y \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $\mathbf{a}$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}^T$ (for stationary points) or $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf{a})$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(\mathbf a),$ we have the following:

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) > 0,$ then:

    • if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $\mathbf{a}$

    • if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) >0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $\mathbf{a}$

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $\mathbf{a}$

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) = 0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \begin{bmatrix} \ln y & \dfrac x y \end{bmatrix},$ we must have

\[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \ln y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac x y. \]

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf{0}^T,$ we obtain the following system:

\[ \begin{cases} \ln y= 0 \\[5pt] \dfrac x y = 0 \end{cases} \]

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get \[ \ln y= 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y=1. \] Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get \[ \dfrac x 1 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=0. \]

Hence, $(0,1)$ is an stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (\ln y) = 0 \qquad & \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left(\dfrac x y\right) = \dfrac 1 y \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(\ln y) = \dfrac 1 y \qquad & \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left (\dfrac x y\right) = -\dfrac {x}{y^2} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, the second derivative is

\begin{align*} \boldsymbol f''(x,y) &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} & \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} \\ \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x} & \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \dfrac {1}{y} \\ \dfrac {1}{y} & -\dfrac {x}{y^2} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,1),$ we obtain \begin{align*} \boldsymbol f''(0,1) = \begin{bmatrix} 0& 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Computing the determinant $H(0,1),$ we get \[ H(0,1) = \det(\boldsymbol f''(0,1)) = 0^2 -1\cdot 1 - = -1 < 0. \] Therefore, $f(0,1)$ is a saddle point.

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,1).$

example.title: Finding and Classifying All Critical Points Using the Second Partial Derivatives Test

question.text:
The function $ f(x,y) % = -2x^2-3y^2+8x-6y-13 $ has the second derivative \[ \boldsymbol f''(x,y) = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix} \] and has a stationary point at $(2,-1).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

  1. $H(2,-1) > 0$
  2. $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(2,-1) > 0 $
  3. The point $(2,-1)$ is a local minimum of $f$
question.explanation:
The second partial derivative test states that if $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(\mathbf a),$ we have the following:

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) > 0,$ then:

    • if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $\mathbf{a}$

    • if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) >0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $\mathbf{a}$

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $\mathbf{a}$

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) = 0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

Evaluating the second derivative at $(2,-1),$ we obtain \begin{align*} \boldsymbol f''(2,-1) = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Now, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of $\boldsymbol f''(2,-1),$ we get \[ H(2,-1) = \det(\boldsymbol f''(2,-1)) = (-4) \cdot (-6) - 0^2 = 24 > 0. \]

  • Statement II is false. We have $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(2,-1) = (\boldsymbol f''(2,-1))_{11} = -4 \lt 0.$

  • Statement III is false. Since $H(2,-1) > 0$ and $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(2,-1) < 0 ,$ the point $(2,-1)$ is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

example.title: Classifying a Critical Point Using the Second Partial Derivatives Test

question.text: Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y) = 4x-6y-x^2-3y^2,$ and determine which of the following statements is true.
question.explanation:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $\mathbf{a}$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}^T$ (for stationary points) or $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf{a})$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(\mathbf a),$ we have the following:

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) > 0,$ then:

    • if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $\mathbf{a}$

    • if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) >0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $\mathbf{a}$

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $\mathbf{a}$

  • If $H(\mathbf{a}) = 0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \boldsymbol f′(x,y) &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (4x-6y-x^2-3y^2) & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(4x-6y-x^2-3y^2) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4-2x & -6-6y \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $\boldsymbol f′(x,y)=\mathbf{0}^T,$ we obtain the following system: \[ \begin{cases} 4-2x = 0 \\[3pt] -6-6y = 0 \end{cases} \] Solving the first equation for $x$, we get \[ 4-2x=0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=2. \] Solving the second equation for $y,$ we get \[ -6-6y=0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y=-1. \] Hence, $(2,-1)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (4-2x) = -2 \qquad & \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (-6-6y) = 0 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} (4-2x) = 0 \qquad & \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} (-6-6y) = -6 \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, the second derivative is

\begin{align*} \boldsymbol f''(x,y)&= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} & \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} \\ \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x} & \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Evaluating the second derivative at $(2,-1),$ we obtain

\begin{align*} \boldsymbol f''(2,-1) = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Computing the determinant $H(2,-1),$ we get \[ H(2,-1) = \det(\boldsymbol f''(2,-1)) = (-2) \cdot (-6) - 0^2 = 12 > 0. \]

Finally, notice that \[ \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(2,-1) = (\boldsymbol f''(2,-1))_{11} = -2 < 0. \]

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(2,-1).$
